decks.title: Loci — Part 1: Circles, parallels and the perpendicular bisector
goals: Explain what a locus is and describe a locus in words
Draw the locus of points at a fixed distance from a point (a circle) and from a line (two parallel lines)
Draw the perpendicular bisector as the locus of points equidistant from two points and use it to find lengths
Check, with distances, whether a point is on a given locus

slides.heading: Loci, Part 1
slides.body_md: A **locus** is the path of a point that obeys a rule. In this part we meet three loci you will draw again and again: the circle, the pair of parallel lines and the perpendicular bisector.

visual.alt: A circle with centre O and four points P, Q, R and S on it. The dashed segments from O to each point carry one tick, showing that all four points are the same distance from O. The circle is the locus of such points.
visual.caption: Points at the same distance from $O$ lie on a circle: the locus.

slides.narration: Welcome to loci. Look at these points. Each one is the same distance from the centre O, so together they sit on a circle. That circle is the locus of a point that stays a fixed distance from O. In this part we study three loci: the circle, a pair of parallel lines, and the perpendicular bisector.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Say what a **locus** is
Draw the locus at a **fixed distance** from a point or a line
Draw the **perpendicular bisector** of a segment
Test whether a point is **on** a locus
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we learn what a locus is. Then we draw the locus of points at a fixed distance from a point, and from a line. Next we construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment, and finally we test whether a given point lies on a locus.

slides.heading: What is a locus?
slides.body_md: A **locus** is the set of **all** the points, and **only** those points, that obey a given rule. It can be a curve, a line, a pair of lines or a region.
bullets: every point of the locus obeys the rule
every point that obeys the rule is on the locus
a locus is drawn, not just described: use a ruler and a pair of compasses

rows: tip of a minute hand, $7$ cm long
centre of a coin rolling along a ruler edge
a line parallel to the edge
a shelter equally far from two bus stops
the perpendicular bisector of the stops
a lamp equally far from two crossing roads

visual.alt: Table of everyday loci: the tip of a seven centimetre minute hand moves on a circle of radius seven centimetres; the centre of a coin rolling along a ruler edge stays one and a half centimetres from the edge, so it moves on a parallel line; a shelter equally far from two bus stops is on the perpendicular bisector of the stops; a lamp equally far from two crossing roads is on one of the two angle bisectors.
visual.caption: A locus is the path a point follows when it obeys a rule.

slides.narration: A locus is the set of all points that obey a rule, and only those points. Every point of the locus obeys the rule, and every point that obeys the rule belongs to the locus. The table shows everyday examples: the tip of a clock hand moves on a circle, and a shelter equally far from two bus stops lies on a special line. We shall learn that line shortly.

slides.heading: Locus 1: a fixed distance from a fixed point
slides.body_md: The points at a fixed distance $r$ from a fixed point $O$ form a **circle** with centre $O$ and radius $r$. Points nearer than $r$ are inside; points farther than $r$ are outside.

visual.alt: A circle of radius 3 centimetres with centre O. Point X is inside, 2 centimetres from O; point P is on the circle, 3 centimetres from O; point Y is outside, 4.2 centimetres from O.
visual.caption: Distance from $O$: $X$ is inside ($2$), $P$ is on the circle ($3$), $Y$ is outside ($4.2$). Lengths in cm.

math: OX < r \text{ (inside)}, \quad OP = r \text{ (on the circle)}, \quad OY > r \text{ (outside)}
slides.narration: The points that stay the same distance from a fixed point O form a circle. The fixed distance is the radius. Point X is two centimetres from O, so it is inside the circle of radius three. Point P is exactly three centimetres away, so it is on the circle. Point Y is four point two centimetres away, so it is outside.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: inside, on or outside?
slides.body_md: A circle has centre $O$ at the origin and radius $3$ cm. Where are $P(1, 2)$, $Q(3, 0)$, $R(-2, 3)$ and $S(-2.4, 1.8)$ (coordinates in cm)?
bullets: **Step 1 —** the squared distance of $(x, y)$ from $O$ is $x^2 + y^2$; compare with $r^2 = 9$.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1: with centre O and radius 3, point P at one, two has squared distance 5 which is less than 9, so it is inside; point Q at three, zero has 9, so it is on the circle; point R at minus two, three has 13, so it is outside; point S at minus two point four, one point eight has 9, so it is on the circle.
visual.caption: Compare the squared distance with $r^2$.

slides.narration: To place a point, work out its squared distance from the centre and compare it with the radius squared, which is nine. For P the squared distance is five, less than nine, so P is inside. Q gives nine exactly, so it is on the circle. R gives thirteen, which is more than nine, so R is outside. S gives five point seven six plus three point two four, which is nine, so S is on the circle.

slides.heading: Quick check: a circle locus
slides.body_md: Name the locus, then say what its centre and radius are.
slides.narration: Read the situation carefully. Decide what stays fixed and what moves, and name the locus.

slides.heading: Locus 2: a fixed distance from a fixed line
slides.body_md: The points at a fixed distance $d$ from a line $l$ lie on **two lines parallel to $l$**, one on each side of $l$, each at distance $d$ from it.
bullets: the two parallels are $2d$ apart
distance from a line is always measured **perpendicular** to the line

visual.alt: A horizontal line l with two parallel lines m and n, one 2 centimetres above and one 2 centimetres below. Point Q on m and point R on n are each joined to l by a perpendicular of length 2 centimetres.
visual.caption: Points $2$ cm from $l$ lie on two parallels, one on each side. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Now take a fixed line instead of a fixed point. Points that stay two centimetres from the line lie on two parallel lines, one above and one below. Distance from a line is measured at a right angle to it, as the dashed segments show. The two parallel lines are four centimetres apart, which is twice the distance.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the path of a coin
slides.body_md: A coin of radius $1.5$ cm rolls along the straight edge of a ruler, staying on one side. Describe the locus of its centre. If the coin could roll along either side of the edge, how far apart would the two paths be?
bullets: **Step 1 —** the coin touches the edge, so its centre is always $1.5$ cm from the edge, measured at right angles.
**Step 2 —** the locus is a **line parallel to the edge**, $1.5$ cm from it, on the side the coin rolls on.
**Step 3 —** with both sides, the two parallels are $1.5 + 1.5 = 3$ cm apart.

visual.alt: A coin of radius 1.5 centimetres rolls along a straight ruler edge. Two positions of the coin are drawn, both touching the edge. The centre C of the coin stays on a dashed line parallel to the edge and 1.5 centimetres above it.
visual.caption: The centre of the coin keeps $1.5$ cm from the edge: it moves on a parallel line. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: When the coin touches the edge, its centre is one and a half centimetres from the edge, which is the radius. So the centre moves on a line parallel to the edge, one and a half centimetres away. If the coin could roll on both sides of the edge, there would be two such lines, one and a half plus one and a half, which is three centimetres apart.

slides.heading: Quick check: a pair of lines
slides.body_md: How many sides of the wall does the locus cover?
slides.narration: Think about which side of the wall the points can be on, and how far each line is from the wall.

slides.heading: Locus 3: equidistant from two points
slides.body_md: The points equally far from two fixed points $A$ and $B$ lie on the **perpendicular bisector** of $AB$: the line through the mid-point $M$ at right angles to $AB$.

visual.alt: A horizontal segment AB of length 6 centimetres with its perpendicular bisector m drawn through the mid-point M. Point P on m above AB and point Q on m below AB are each joined to A and B by dashed segments; the segments to A and B from the same point carry the same number of ticks, so PA equals PB and QA equals QB.
visual.caption: Every point of the perpendicular bisector $m$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$: $PA = PB$ and $QA = QB$. Length in cm.

math: PA = PB \iff P \text{ is on the perpendicular bisector of } AB
slides.narration: Next, the points that are equally far from two fixed points A and B. These lie on the perpendicular bisector of A B. That is the line through the mid point at a right angle to A B. Point P is joined to A and B and the two dashed segments have the same length. The same is true for Q below the line. Every point of the bisector works, and no other point does.

slides.heading: Drawing the perpendicular bisector
slides.body_md: With compasses and a ruler: draw $AB$. From $A$ and from $B$ draw arcs of the **same radius**, more than half of $AB$, meeting at $X$ and $Y$. Join $XY$.
bullets: the radius must be **greater than half** of $AB$ or the arcs do not cross
$XY$ meets $AB$ at its mid-point $M$, at a right angle
every point of $XY$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$

visual.alt: Segment AB of length 5 centimetres. A circle of radius 3.5 centimetres is drawn about A and another about B; they meet at X above AB and Y below AB. The line XY crosses AB at its mid-point M at a right angle.
visual.caption: Arcs of equal radius (more than half of $AB$) from $A$ and $B$ meet at $X$ and $Y$; $XY$ is the perpendicular bisector. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: To draw the perpendicular bisector, set your compasses to more than half of A B. Draw arcs from A and from B with this same radius. They cross at two points, X above and Y below. Join X and Y with a ruler. This line cuts A B at its mid point, at a right angle. If the radius is too small the arcs never meet.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a point on the bisector
slides.body_md: $A$ and $B$ are $6$ cm apart. $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ and $PA = 5$ cm. Find the distance of $P$ from $AB$, and the distance between $P$ and the point $Q$ on the other side of $AB$ with $QA = 5$ cm.
bullets: **Step 1 —** the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ is the mid-point $M$, and $AM = 3$ cm.
**Step 2 —** in the right triangle $AMP$: $PM = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ cm.
**Step 3 —** $Q$ is the same distance below $AB$, so $PQ = 4 + 4 = 8$ cm.

visual.alt: Worked example: A and B are 6 centimetres apart. P and Q lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, each 5 centimetres from A and from B. The distance PM from P to the mid-point M is 4 centimetres.
visual.caption: Given $AB = 6$ and $PA = PB = 5$ (cm). The right triangle $AMP$ has $AM = 3$, $AP = 5$, so $PM = 4$.

slides.narration: The foot of the perpendicular from P is the mid point M of A B, so A M is three centimetres. The triangle A M P has a right angle at M. So P M is the square root of five squared minus three squared, which is the square root of sixteen, or four centimetres. The point Q is four centimetres below A B, so P Q is four plus four, which is eight centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: the shelter
slides.body_md: Which line is equally far from two points?
slides.narration: Remember what the locus of points equally far from two fixed points is called, and where it crosses the segment joining them.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: testing points on a coordinate plan
slides.body_md: On a plan $A$ is $(-2, 1)$ and $B$ is $(6, 1)$. Show that $(2, 5)$ and $(2, -3)$ are equidistant from $A$ and $B$, but $(3, 1)$ and $(0, 4)$ are not.
bullets: **Step 1 —** the mid-point of $AB$ has $x = \dfrac{-2 + 6}{2} = 2$, so the locus is the line $x = 2$.
**Step 2 —** $(2, 5)$: $PA^2 = 4^2 + 4^2 = 32 = PB^2$. The point $(2, -3)$ gives the same.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 4: A is at minus two, one and B at six, one, so the locus is the line x equals two. The points two, five and two, minus three have PA squared equal to PB squared equal to 32 and are on the locus; the points three, one and zero, four have unequal squared distances and are not.
visual.caption: The locus of points equidistant from $A(-2, 1)$ and $B(6, 1)$ is the line $x = 2$.

slides.narration: The points A and B have the same height, so the perpendicular bisector is the vertical line through the mid point. The mid point has x equal to two, so the locus is the line x equals two. Points on it, like two comma five, are the same distance from A and from B. Points off it, like three comma one, are not: their squared distances are twenty five and nine.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Fixed distance from a **point**: a circle
Fixed distance from a **line**: two parallel lines, one on each side
Equidistant from two **points**: the perpendicular bisector
Distances from a line are measured **at right angles**

rows: a fixed distance $r$ from a fixed point $O$
a fixed distance $d$ from a fixed line $l$
two lines parallel to $l$, $d$ from it on each side

visual.alt: Summary table for part one: a fixed distance from a fixed point gives a circle; a fixed distance from a fixed line gives two parallel lines, one on each side; equal distance from two fixed points gives the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A fixed distance from a point gives a circle. A fixed distance from a line gives two parallel lines, one on each side. Equal distances from two points give the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Always measure distance from a line at a right angle.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Name the locus (1 mark):** circle, pair of parallels or perpendicular bisector, with the distance or points
**Construction (1–2 marks):** compass arcs left visible, a sharp pencil, labelled points
**Radius for the bisector:** more than half the segment
**Mistake:** drawing only **one** parallel when the distance is on both sides
**Mistake:** measuring distance from a line along a slant
**Habit:** do not rub out construction arcs
slides.narration: In the exam, name the locus and give its distance or its points. Leave your compass arcs visible, because the marks are for the construction. For the perpendicular bisector use a radius of more than half the segment. Common slips are drawing only one of the two parallel lines, and measuring distance from a line along a slant instead of at a right angle.

decks.title: Loci — Part 2: Angle bisectors, midlines and combined loci
goals: Draw the angle bisector and use it as the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines
Draw the locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines
Find a point that satisfies two conditions as the intersection of two loci, and count the solutions
Solve construction problems: construct, draw the loci, mark the points and measure

slides.heading: Loci, Part 2
slides.body_md: Two lines that cross have **two** angle bisectors, and every point on them is equally far from both lines. Combining loci lets us locate points that obey two rules at once.

visual.alt: Two lines p and q meet at O at an angle of 50 degrees. The dashed line b bisects that angle. Point X on b is joined by perpendiculars to p and to q; the two perpendiculars carry one tick each, so they are equal.
visual.caption: Every point of the bisector $b$ is the same distance from the two lines $p$ and $q$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Two lines cross, and the dashed line bisects the angle between them. The point X on the bisector is joined to each line by a perpendicular, and the two perpendiculars are equal. So the bisector is the locus of points equally far from both lines. Then we combine loci to solve construction problems.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Draw the **angle bisector** and use it as a locus
Find the locus **between two parallel lines**
Locate points by **intersecting** two loci
Solve a **construction problem** and measure the answer
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We draw the angle bisector and use it as a locus. We find the line midway between two parallel lines. We locate points where two loci meet, and we solve construction problems by drawing, marking and measuring.

slides.heading: Locus 4: equidistant from two intersecting lines
slides.body_md: The points equally far from two lines that cross at $O$ lie on the **bisectors of the angles** between them. Every point of a bisector is the same distance from the two lines.
bullets: distance to each line is measured at a **right angle**

visual.alt: Two lines p and q meet at O at an angle of 50 degrees. The dashed line b bisects that angle. Point X on b is joined by perpendiculars to p and to q; the two perpendiculars carry one tick each, so they are equal.
visual.caption: Every point of the bisector $b$ is the same distance from the two lines $p$ and $q$.

math: \text{point on a bisector} \Rightarrow \text{distance to } p = \text{distance to } q
slides.narration: Here is the fourth locus. Points that are equally far from two crossing lines lie on the bisectors of the angles between the lines. The two perpendiculars from the point X to the lines carry a tick mark each, because they are equal. This is true for every point on the bisector, not just X.

slides.heading: Drawing an angle bisector
slides.body_md: Place the compass point at $O$ and cut both arms at $P$ and $Q$. From $P$ and $Q$ draw equal arcs that meet at $R$. Join $OR$: it bisects the angle.
bullets: the arcs from $P$ and $Q$ must have the **same** radius
$OR$ makes two **equal** angles with the arms

visual.alt: An angle AOB of 70 degrees. A circle about O cuts the arms at P and Q. Equal circles about P and Q meet at R. The dashed line OR bisects the angle, giving two angles of 35 degrees.
visual.caption: Steps: arc from $O$ cuts the arms at $P$, $Q$; equal arcs from $P$ and $Q$ meet at $R$; $OR$ bisects $\angle AOB$.

slides.narration: To bisect an angle, put the compass point on the vertex O and draw an arc that cuts both arms, at P and Q. Then, with the same radius from P and from Q, draw two arcs that cross at R. A ruler line from O through R splits the seventy degree angle into two angles of thirty five degrees.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: distance from the arms
slides.body_md: The angle $ABC$ is $70^\circ$. $P$ is on its bisector, $4$ cm from $B$. Find the angle between $BP$ and each arm, and the distance of $P$ from each arm (to $0.1$ cm).
bullets: **Step 1 —** the bisector halves the angle: $\dfrac{70}{2} = 35^\circ$ with each arm.
**Step 2 —** the perpendicular from $P$ to an arm and $BP$ form a right triangle with hypotenuse $4$.
**Step 3 —** the distance is $4 \sin 35^\circ \approx 2.3$ cm, the same for both arms.

visual.alt: An angle ABC of 70 degrees with its bisector drawn as a dashed line. Point P on the bisector is 4 centimetres from B, and the two perpendiculars from P to the arms BA and BC carry one tick each, so they are equal.
visual.caption: Each half of the $70^\circ$ angle is $35^\circ$. $BP = 4$ cm; the perpendiculars from $P$ to the arms are equal. Length in cm.

slides.narration: The bisector halves the seventy degree angle, so it makes thirty five degrees with each arm. The perpendicular from P to an arm, together with B P and part of the arm, forms a right triangle whose longest side is four centimetres. The distance is four times the sine of thirty five degrees, which is about two point three centimetres, the same for both arms.

slides.heading: Quick check: two crossing paths
slides.body_md: How many lines make up the locus?
slides.narration: Remember that two crossing lines make two pairs of vertically opposite angles.

slides.heading: The two bisectors are at right angles
slides.body_md: Two lines that cross make two different angles, $\theta$ and $180^\circ - \theta$. Each has a bisector, and the two bisectors meet at $\dfrac{\theta}{2} + \dfrac{180^\circ - \theta}{2} = 90^\circ$.
bullets: the **full locus** is the pair of bisectors
on each bisector the distance to the two lines is the same

visual.alt: Two lines p and q crossing at O at 50 degrees, with both angle bisectors drawn dashed. The bisector b of the 50 degree angle and the bisector c of the 130 degree angle meet at O at a right angle, which is marked.
visual.caption: The locus is a pair of lines, $b$ and $c$, at right angles to each other.

slides.narration: The full locus of points equally far from two crossing lines is a pair of lines, the two angle bisectors. Here the lines cross at fifty degrees. One bisector halves fifty degrees, the other halves the neighbouring one hundred and thirty degrees. Half of fifty plus half of one hundred and thirty is ninety, so the two bisectors always meet at a right angle.

slides.heading: Locus 5: equidistant from two parallel lines
slides.body_md: The points equally far from two parallel lines $l$ and $m$ lie on a line **parallel to both**, midway between them. If $l$ and $m$ are $g$ apart, it is $\dfrac{g}{2}$ from each.

visual.alt: Two parallel lines l and m, 4 centimetres apart, with a dashed line n halfway between them. Point X on n is joined by perpendiculars of length 2 centimetres to l and to m.
visual.caption: Points equidistant from the parallels $l$ and $m$ lie on the line $n$ halfway between them. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: The last standard locus uses two parallel lines. Points equally far from both lie on a third parallel line, exactly halfway between them. Here the lines l and m are four centimetres apart, so the dashed line n is two centimetres from each, as the perpendiculars from the point X show.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a line of lamps
slides.body_md: The two edges of a straight canal path are parallel and $3.6$ m apart. A line of lamps is to be equally far from both edges. Describe where it goes.
bullets: **Step 1 —** the locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines is a **third parallel line** midway between them.
**Step 2 —** its distance from each edge is $\dfrac{3.6}{2} = 1.8$ m.
**Step 3 —** draw the edges $3.6$ cm apart (scale $1$ cm to $1$ m) and the line $1.8$ cm from each.

visual.alt: Worked example: two parallel lines l and m are 3.6 centimetres apart. The dashed line n halfway between them is 1.8 centimetres from each.
visual.caption: Lines $l$ and $m$ are $3.6$ cm apart: the locus $n$ is $1.8$ cm from each. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Points equally far from two parallel lines lie on a third parallel line halfway between them. The edges are three point six metres apart, so the line of lamps is half of that, one point eight metres, from each edge. On a drawing with one centimetre to one metre, draw the edges three point six centimetres apart and the middle line one point eight centimetres from each.

slides.heading: Intersection of loci
slides.body_md: A point that obeys **two** conditions lies on **both** loci, so it is where the two loci **intersect**. The number of solutions is the number of common points: a line and a circle can meet in $2$, $1$ or $0$ points.

visual.alt: A circle with centre A and radius 3 centimetres and three horizontal lines. Line p cuts the circle at two points X and Y, line q just touches it at T, and line s misses it altogether.
visual.caption: A line and a circle can have $2$, $1$ or $0$ points in common: so two loci can give $2$, $1$ or $0$ solutions.

slides.narration: A point that obeys two rules lies on both loci, so we look for the points where the two loci cross. A line and a circle can cross at two points, like line p, touch at one point, like line q, or miss each other completely, like line s. So a problem with two conditions can have two solutions, one solution or none.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: equidistant and a fixed distance
slides.body_md: $A$ and $B$ are $4$ cm apart. Find the points that are equally far from $A$ and $B$ and $3$ cm from $A$, and measure the distance between them.
bullets: **Step 1 —** locus 1: the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, $\dfrac{4}{2} = 2$ cm from $A$ along $AB$. Locus 2: a circle of radius $3$ cm about $A$.
**Step 2 —** they meet at $P$ and $Q$ on either side of $AB$, each $\sqrt{3^2 - 2^2} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$ cm from $AB$.
**Step 3 —** measuring gives $PQ = 2 \times 2.24 \approx 4.5$ cm.

visual.alt: A and B are 4 centimetres apart. A circle of radius 3 centimetres is drawn about A, and the perpendicular bisector m of AB is drawn. They meet at P above AB and Q below it, and each of these is 3 centimetres from A and from B.
visual.caption: Locus 1: circle, radius $3$ about $A$. Locus 2: perpendicular bisector $m$ of $AB$. They meet at $P$ and $Q$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Draw the perpendicular bisector of A B, which crosses A B two centimetres from A. Then draw a circle of radius three centimetres about A. They meet at two points, P above and Q below. Each is the square root of nine minus four, about two point two four centimetres, from A B. So P Q is about four point five centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: how many points?
slides.body_md: Do the two circles meet?
slides.narration: Compare the distance between the two centres with the sum and the difference of the radii.

slides.heading: Method for a construction problem
slides.body_md: Always follow the same plan, and keep every construction line.
bullets: **construct** the given figure to the stated measurements
draw each **locus** with ruler and compasses
the required point is where the loci **intersect**
measure with a ruler or protractor and write the answer **with units**

nodes.label: Read the conditions on the point
Draw the given figure to scale
Draw the locus for each condition

visual.alt: Flow chart for a construction problem: read the conditions, draw the given figure to scale, draw the locus for each condition, mark where the loci meet, then measure and write the answer.
visual.caption: A point that obeys two conditions lies on both loci.

slides.narration: Every construction problem follows the same plan. First draw the given figure to the measurements stated. Then draw the locus for each condition using a ruler and compasses. Mark the point or points where the loci meet. Finally measure what the question asks for, and write the answer with its units. Keep all your construction lines.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: bisector and perpendicular bisector
slides.body_md: Construct triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 6.5$ cm, $\angle B = 60^\circ$ and $AB = 5$ cm. Locate $P$ equidistant from $BA$ and $BC$ and also from $B$ and $C$. Measure $BP$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** locus 1: the bisector of $\angle B$, $30^\circ$ with each arm. Locus 2: the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, through $M$ with $BM = \dfrac{6.5}{2} = 3.25$ cm.
**Step 2 —** the loci meet at $P$, inside the triangle.
**Step 3 —** in the right triangle $BMP$, $BP = \dfrac{3.25}{\cos 30^\circ} \approx 3.8$ cm.

visual.alt: Worked example 4: triangle ABC with BC 6.5 centimetres, AB 5 centimetres and angle B 60 degrees. The dashed bisector of angle B and the dashed perpendicular bisector of BC meet at P inside the triangle. M is the mid-point of BC and each half of angle B is 30 degrees.
visual.caption: Loci: bisector of $\angle B$ and perpendicular bisector of $BC$ meet at $P$. Lengths in cm.

slides.narration: Construct the triangle first. Locus one is the bisector of angle B, which makes thirty degrees with each arm. Locus two is the perpendicular bisector of B C, through the mid point M, three point two five centimetres from B. They meet at P. In the right triangle B M P, B P is three point two five divided by the cosine of thirty degrees, which measures about three point eight centimetres.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: bisector and a parallel
slides.body_md: Construct triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 7$ cm, $CA = 5$ cm and $AB = 6$ cm. Locate $P$ inside the triangle equally far from $AB$ and $AC$ and $2$ cm from $BC$. Measure $AP$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** locus 1: the bisector of $\angle A$. Locus 2: the line parallel to $BC$ and $2$ cm from it, inside the triangle.
**Step 2 —** mark $P$ where they meet.
**Step 3 —** measuring gives $AP = 2.2$ cm, and $P$ is $1.4$ cm from $AB$ and from $AC$.

sections.heading: 1. What a locus is; the circle
sections.body_md:
- A **locus** is the set of **all** the points, and **only** those points, that obey a given rule: a curve, a line, a pair of lines or a region.
- **Fixed distance from a fixed point** $O$: a **circle** with centre $O$ and that distance as radius.
- Inside: $OX < r$; on the circle: $OP = r$; outside: $OY > r$. With coordinates, compare $x^2 + y^2$ with $r^2$.
- Drawing at a scale: a real radius $R$ drawn at $1 : n$ has radius $\dfrac{R}{n}$ on the plan.

*Example:* the tip of a $7$ cm minute hand is always $7$ cm from the pivot: a circle of radius $7$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: The set of all points, and only those points, that satisfy a given condition.
Points at a fixed distance (the radius) from a fixed point (the centre).

visuals.caption: Points at the same distance from $O$ lie on a circle: the locus.

sections.heading: 2. Fixed distance from a line
sections.body_md:
- The points at a fixed distance $d$ from a line $l$ form **two lines parallel to $l$**, one on each side, each at distance $d$.
- Distance from a line is measured **at right angles** to the line.
- The two parallels are $2d$ apart; if only one side is allowed, only one parallel is the locus.

*Example:* a coin of radius $1.5$ cm rolling along an edge has its centre on a line parallel to the edge and $1.5$ cm from it.

key_terms.definition_md: The pair of lines parallel to a given line, at a given distance on either side of it.

sections.heading: 3. Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector
sections.body_md:
- The points equally far from $A$ and $B$ lie on the **perpendicular bisector** of $AB$: it passes through the mid-point $M$ at right angles to $AB$.
- **Construction:** arcs of equal radius (more than $\dfrac{AB}{2}$) from $A$ and from $B$ meet at $X$ and $Y$; join $XY$.
- A point $P$ on the bisector has $PM = \sqrt{PA^2 - AM^2}$.
- The proofs of the locus theorems are not in the ICSE 2027 syllabus: the results are used.

*Example:* $AB = 6$, $PA = 5$: $PM = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: The line through the mid-point of a segment, at right angles to it; the locus of points equidistant from its ends.

formulas.label: P on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$

Point P on m above AB and point Q on m below AB are each joined to A and B by dashed segments; the segments to A and B from the same point carry the same number of ticks, so PA equals PB and QA equals QB.
visual.caption: Every point of the perpendicular bisector $m$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$: $PA = PB$ and $QA = QB$. Length in cm.

sections.heading: 4. Equidistant from two intersecting lines: angle bisectors
sections.body_md:
- The points equally far from two lines that cross lie on the **bisectors of the angles** between them: **two** lines.
- The two bisectors are **at right angles**: $\dfrac{\theta}{2} + \dfrac{180^\circ - \theta}{2} = 90^\circ$.
- **Construction:** arcs from the vertex cut the arms at $P$, $Q$; equal arcs from $P$ and $Q$ meet at $R$; join the vertex to $R$.
- A point on a bisector at distance $s$ from the vertex is $s \sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ from each arm.

*Example:* an angle of $70^\circ$, $P$ at $4$ cm on its bisector: distance $4 \sin 35^\circ \approx 2.3$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: The line that divides an angle into two equal angles; the locus of points equidistant from the arms.

formulas.label: Distance from a point on the bisector to an arm

visual.caption: Every point of the bisector $b$ is the same distance from the two lines $p$ and $q$.

sections.heading: 5. Equidistant from two parallel lines
sections.body_md:
- The points equally far from two parallel lines lie on **one line parallel to both**, midway between them.
- If the lines are $g$ apart, the middle line is $\dfrac{g}{2}$ from each.
- Two parallels have no crossing point, so there is just one locus line (unlike crossing lines, which give two).

*Example:* edges $3.6$ m apart: the line of lamps is $1.8$ m from each edge.

key_terms.definition_md: The line parallel to two given parallel lines and halfway between them.

sections.heading: 6. Intersection of loci
sections.body_md:
- A point that obeys **two** conditions lies on **both** loci: it is where they **intersect**.
- A line and a circle meet in **2**, **1** or **0** points (secant, tangent, no contact); two circles meet in $2$ points if $|r_1 - r_2| < d < r_1 + r_2$, in $1$ point if $d = r_1 + r_2$ (or $|r_1 - r_2|$), and in none otherwise ($d$ is the distance between centres).
- Always ask: how many solutions are there? Does each one satisfy every condition (for example, inside the triangle)?

*Example:* $A$, $B$ $4$ cm apart; points $3$ cm from $A$ and equidistant from $A$ and $B$: $2$ points, $PQ \approx 4.5$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: The set of points common to two loci: the points that obey both conditions.

sections.heading: 7. Construction problems
sections.body_md:
- **Plan:** (1) construct the given figure, (2) draw each locus, (3) mark the point where they meet, (4) measure and answer with units.
- Keep all construction arcs; use a sharp pencil; label every point.
- Typical pairs: bisector of an angle with the perpendicular bisector of a side; bisector with a line parallel to a side; a circle with a perpendicular bisector; two perpendicular bisectors (the point equidistant from three corners).
- **Regions:** "nearer to $B$ than to $C$" is one side of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$; "within $r$ of $A$" is inside a circle.

*Example:* triangle $BC = 6.5$, $\angle B = 60^\circ$, $AB = 5$: the bisector of $B$ meets the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ at $P$ with $BP \approx 3.8$ cm.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Naming a locus (1–2 marks):* the right figure (circle, pair of parallels, perpendicular bisector, angle bisectors, midline) with its distance or points.
- *Construction (2–3 marks):* given figure with exact lengths and angles 1–2; each locus 1; arcs left visible.
- *Point and measurement (2–3 marks):* point marked and labelled 1; measured length or angle with units 1–2 (within $0.1$ cm or $1^\circ$).
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually $3 + 3 + 4$; the figure first, the loci next, the measurements last.

**Common mistakes**
1. Drawing only one parallel when the distance is on both sides of the line, or only one bisector of two crossing lines.
2. Using a radius less than half the segment when drawing the perpendicular bisector.
3. Measuring a distance from a line along a slant instead of at a right angle.
4. Rubbing out the construction arcs, which loses the construction marks.
5. Forgetting that a circle and a line (or a bisector) can meet in two points, giving two answers; or that they may not meet at all.
6. Accepting a point that obeys the two loci but lies outside the figure the question restricts it to.

questions.stem_md: In the chapter on loci, what does the "locus" of a moving point mean?

options.text_md: the set of all points, and only those points, that satisfy the given condition
the longest segment that can be drawn in the figure
the angle between the path and a fixed line
the single point where two paths cross

questions.solution_md: A locus is a set of points: every point of the set satisfies the condition, and every point that satisfies the condition is in the set. It is a path or a region (a circle, a line, a pair of lines), not one point, one segment or one angle.

questions.stem_md: A lamp on a pole lights every spot on level ground that is exactly $6$ m from the foot of the pole. What is the locus of the spots lit at exactly that distance?

options.text_md: a disc of radius $12$ m about the pole
a circle of radius $6$ m with the foot of the pole as centre
a straight line $6$ m from the pole
two parallel lines, each $6$ m from the pole

questions.solution_md: The points at a fixed distance from a fixed point form a circle with that point as centre and the distance as radius. Every point of the circle is $6$ m from the pole and no other point is. A line or a pair of lines cannot stay a constant distance from a point, and a disc contains points nearer than $6$ m.

questions.stem_md: Bus stops $S$ and $T$ are on a straight road. A shelter is to stand at a spot equally far from $S$ and from $T$. The possible spots form

options.text_md: a line parallel to $ST$ through its mid-point

questions.solution_md: The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. The mid-point of $ST$ is on it, but the line $ST$ itself is not (its points are not equally far from $S$ and $T$ except the mid-point), and a line parallel to $ST$ would never cross the bisector at right angles.

questions.stem_md: Two straight footpaths cross at a junction. What is the locus of the points that are equally far from both footpaths?

options.text_md: a line parallel to both footpaths
one line only: the bisector of the smaller angle
the two lines that bisect the angles between the footpaths

questions.solution_md: A point equidistant from two intersecting lines lies on an angle bisector. The two lines make two pairs of vertically opposite angles, and each pair has its own bisector, so the locus is a pair of lines, not one line. It is never a circle or a parallel line.

questions.stem_md: The two rails of a straight railway track are $1.5$ m apart. Points that are the same distance from each rail lie on

options.text_md: a line parallel to the rails, $0.75$ m from each
a line parallel to the rails, $1.5$ m from each
two lines parallel to the rails, $0.75$ m from the nearer rail on the outside
a line at right angles to the rails

questions.solution_md: The locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines is the parallel line midway between them. The gap is $1.5$ m, so the middle line is $\dfrac{1.5}{2} = 0.75$ m from each rail.

questions.stem_md: A boundary wall is straight. On level ground, the locus of points exactly $4$ m from the wall (on either side) is

options.text_md: a circle of radius $4$ m about the middle of the wall
two lines parallel to the wall, one on each side, each $4$ m from it
two lines parallel to the wall, each $2$ m from it
a single line parallel to the wall, $4$ m from it

questions.solution_md: Points at a fixed distance from a line are on two parallel lines, one on each side of it. Each is $4$ m from the wall, so the lines are $8$ m apart. A single line would cover only one side, and a circle is the locus for a fixed point, not a fixed line.

questions.stem_md: Villages $P$ and $Q$ are $18$ km apart on a straight canal bank. A clinic is on the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$ and $15$ km from $P$. How far is the clinic from the canal bank $PQ$?
questions.solution_md: The clinic is above the mid-point $M$ of $PQ$, with $PM = 9$ km, so the clinic, $M$ and $P$ form a right triangle with hypotenuse $15$: $\sqrt{15^2 - 9^2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$ km. The value $6$ is $15 - 9$, $17.5$ is $\sqrt{15^2 + 9^2}$ rounded, and $9$ is the half-length $PM$ itself.

questions.stem_md: Two walls meet in a corner at an angle of $50^\circ$. A sensor on the line that bisects this angle is $8$ m from the corner. To the nearest $0.1$ m, how far is the sensor from each wall?
questions.solution_md: The bisector makes $25^\circ$ with each wall, and the perpendicular from the sensor to a wall is the side opposite $25^\circ$ in a right triangle with hypotenuse $8$: $8 \sin 25^\circ = 3.4$ m. The value $7.3$ is $8 \cos 25^\circ$, $6.1$ uses the whole angle ($8 \sin 50^\circ$) and $4.0$ halves the distance from the corner.

questions.stem_md: A sprinkler at $A$ and a tap at $B$ are $4$ m apart. A seedling is to be planted $3$ m from the sprinkler and $3$ m from the tap. How many positions are possible?
questions.solution_md: Such a point lies on the circle of radius $3$ about $A$ and on the circle of radius $3$ about $B$. The centres are $4$ apart, which is less than $3 + 3 = 6$ and more than $3 - 3 = 0$, so the circles cut in $2$ points, one on each side of $AB$.

questions.stem_md: Two lamp posts stand $8$ m apart. A kiosk is to be the same distance $r$ from both posts. For which value of $r$ is there exactly one possible position for the kiosk?
questions.solution_md: The kiosk is on the circle of radius $r$ about each post, and the two circles have exactly one common point when they touch, that is when $r + r = 8$, so $r = 4$ m. For $r = 3$ m the circles are $8 > 3 + 3$ apart and do not meet; for $r = 8$ m and $r = 5$ m they cut in two points.

questions.stem_md: $C$ is a point on a long straight fence $l$. A surveyor needs pegs that are $2.5$ m from the fence and $3$ m from $C$. How many peg positions are there?
questions.solution_md: Pegs $2.5$ m from the fence lie on two lines parallel to it, one on each side. The circle of radius $3$ about $C$ reaches each of them, because $2.5 < 3$, and cuts each in $2$ points. That gives $2 + 2 = 4$ positions.

questions.stem_md: Two crossing laser beams meet at the point $O$. The locus of the points that are the same distance from both beams is a pair of lines. At what angle do these two lines meet?
questions.solution_md: The two bisectors cut the straight angle on a line into two halves that add up to $\dfrac{180^\circ}{2} = 90^\circ$: if the beams make $\theta$ and $180^\circ - \theta$, the bisectors are $\dfrac{\theta}{2} + \dfrac{180^\circ - \theta}{2} = 90^\circ$ apart. So the pair of lines are always perpendicular, whatever the angle between the beams.

questions.stem_md: Two straight roads cross at $60^\circ$. A fire station is to be equally far from both roads and $5$ km from the crossing. How many sites can it have?
questions.solution_md: Equidistant from both roads means on one of the two angle bisectors. A circle of radius $5$ km about the crossing meets each bisector, which passes through the centre, in $2$ points. So there are $2 + 2 = 4$ sites.

questions.stem_md: A rotating sprinkler waters up to $2.5$ m from its post. On a garden plan drawn so that $1$ cm stands for $0.5$ m, the edge of the watered region is drawn as a circle of radius
questions.solution_md: The locus is a circle of real radius $2.5$ m. On the plan each $0.5$ m becomes $1$ cm, so the radius is $\dfrac{2.5}{0.5} = 5$ cm. The value $1.25$ multiplies instead of dividing, $2.5$ ignores the scale and $10$ is the diameter.

questions.stem_md: To construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment $PQ = 7$ cm with a pair of compasses, the radius used for the arcs drawn from $P$ and from $Q$ must be
questions.solution_md: The arcs from $P$ and $Q$ must cross, which needs the radius to exceed half of $PQ$, that is $\dfrac{7}{2} = 3.5$ cm. At exactly $3.5$ cm the arcs only touch at the mid-point, which is one point, not two, so the bisecting line cannot be drawn; at a smaller radius they do not meet at all.

questions.stem_md: In a coordinate plan, $A(2, 1)$ and $B(8, 1)$ are two survey pegs. A third peg $P$ is the same distance from $A$ and from $B$ and $5$ units from $A$, with a positive $y$-coordinate. The coordinates of $P$ are
questions.solution_md: Equal distances from $A$ and $B$ put $P$ on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, the vertical line $x = 5$. Then $PA^2 = (5 - 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 25$ gives $(y - 1)^2 = 16$, so $y = 5$ (taking the positive value). The point $(5, -3)$ is the other solution, $(5, 6)$ adds $5$ to $y = 1$ and $(6, 5)$ moves off the bisector.

questions.stem_md: Two straight canal banks are parallel and $8$ m apart. A buoy is to be the same distance from both banks and $3$ m from one of them. How many positions can the buoy have?
questions.solution_md: Equidistant from the banks means on the middle line, which is $\dfrac{8}{2} = 4$ m from each bank. A buoy on that line is $4$ m from each bank, never $3$ m. The conditions cannot hold together, so there are $0$ positions.

questions.stem_md: In a coordinate plan the corners of a plot are $A(0, 0)$, $B(6, 0)$ and $C(0, 8)$. A water tank is to be the same distance from $A$, $B$ and $C$. Where does it stand?
questions.solution_md: Equal distance from $A$ and $B$ puts the tank on the line $x = 3$; equal distance from $A$ and $C$ puts it on $y = 4$. These perpendicular bisectors meet at $(3, 4)$, and $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, $\sqrt{(6 - 3)^2 + 4^2} = 5$, $\sqrt{3^2 + (8 - 4)^2} = 5$ confirm it. The points $(3, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$ are the mid-points of $AB$ and $AC$, each on only one bisector.

questions.stem_md: Two crossing roads make an angle at a junction. The line that divides this angle into two equal angles is called the
questions.solution_md: The line through the vertex that splits an angle into two equal parts is the angle bisector, and it is the locus of points equidistant from the arms. A perpendicular bisector belongs to a segment, a median to a triangle, and a tangent to a circle.

questions.stem_md: A security camera at $C$ can see every spot on level ground that is at most $5$ m from $C$. The set of all the spots it can see is

options.text_md: the circle of radius $5$ m only
the region outside the circle of radius $5$ m
a disc: the circle of radius $5$ m together with all the points inside it

questions.solution_md: "At most $5$ m" includes the spots exactly $5$ m away, which form the circle, and all the nearer spots inside it, so the set is the circle together with its inside. The circle alone would be "exactly $5$ m", and the outside is "more than $5$ m".

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The perpendicular bisector of a segment $AB$ passes through the mid-point of $AB$.

**Reason (R):** The locus of points that are equidistant from $A$ and from $B$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true, and so is R. The mid-point $M$ of $AB$ is the same distance from $A$ and from $B$, so by R it lies on the locus, which is the perpendicular bisector. So R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines $6$ cm apart is a line parallel to both, $3$ cm from each.

**Reason (R):** The locus of points equidistant from any two straight lines is a pair of lines that cross at right angles.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: the middle line is $\dfrac{6}{2} = 3$ cm from each. R is false: it is the rule for lines that intersect. Two parallel lines have no point of intersection and give a single middle line, not a crossing pair.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The locus of the points $3$ cm from a straight line $l$ is a single line parallel to $l$.

**Reason (R):** Points that are $3$ cm from $l$ can lie on either side of $l$, so they form two lines parallel to $l$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true: one parallel line on each side of $l$. A is false, because it leaves out the second parallel; the locus is a pair of lines $6$ cm apart.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The two lines that bisect the angles between two intersecting lines are perpendicular to each other.

**Reason (R):** Every point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the two arms of the angle.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. R tells us what is special about the points of one bisector; the perpendicularity of the two bisectors comes from adding the half-angles of a straight line, $\dfrac{\theta}{2} + \dfrac{180^\circ - \theta}{2} = 90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If $AB = 8$ cm, no point is $2$ cm from $A$ and $3$ cm from $B$.

**Reason (R):** A point that is $2$ cm from $A$ and $3$ cm from $B$ can only exist if $AB$ is at most $2 + 3 = 5$ cm.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: The point would lie on a circle of radius $2$ about $A$ and a circle of radius $3$ about $B$. For $AB = 8$ these circles are $8 > 2 + 3$ apart, so they do not meet; R states exactly this condition, so it explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every circle that passes through two points $A$ and $B$ has its centre on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

**Reason (R):** Every point of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is $\dfrac{AB}{2}$ from $A$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true: the centre is the same distance (the radius) from $A$ and from $B$. R is false: only the mid-point $M$ is $\dfrac{AB}{2}$ from $A$. For $A(0, 0)$, $B(6, 0)$ the point $(3, 4)$ is on the bisector but $5$ from $A$, not $3$.

questions.stem_md: The tip of a minute hand $7$ cm long, as the hand turns round a clock face, traces a circle of radius $7$ cm.
questions.solution_md: True. The tip is always $7$ cm from the pivot, so it moves along the locus of points at a fixed distance from a fixed point: a circle with the pivot as centre and radius $7$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The locus of the points equally far from two lines that cross each other is a single straight line.
questions.solution_md: False. Crossing lines form two pairs of vertically opposite angles, and each pair has its own bisector, so the locus is two lines (at right angles to each other).

questions.stem_md: A point $P$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$ exactly when $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
questions.solution_md: True, in both directions: a point of the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from $A$ and $B$, and a point with $PA = PB$ cannot be anywhere else, since it is on the bisector. This is the definition of the locus.

questions.stem_md: A circle of radius $3$ cm about one lamp post and a circle of radius $4$ cm about another post, $8$ cm away, cut each other in two points.
questions.solution_md: False. The radii add up to $3 + 4 = 7$ cm, which is less than the $8$ cm between the centres, so the circles lie apart and have no common point.

questions.stem_md: The perpendicular bisector of a chord of a circle passes through the centre of the circle.
questions.solution_md: True. The centre is the same distance (the radius) from the two ends of the chord, so by the locus of points equidistant from two points it lies on the perpendicular bisector of the chord.

questions.stem_md: A circle of radius $3$ cm drawn about a point $C$ on a line $l$ meets the pair of lines parallel to $l$ and $2$ cm from it in four points altogether.
questions.solution_md: True. The two parallels are $2$ cm from $l$ and $2 < 3$, so the circle cuts each of them in $2$ points: $2 + 2 = 4$ points.

questions.stem_md: Two parallel kerbs have exactly one line of points that are equally far from both of them.
questions.solution_md: True. The points equidistant from two parallel lines lie on the single line parallel to both and midway between them; unlike crossing lines, parallel lines have no second bisector.

questions.stem_md: The perpendicular bisector of a segment $AB$ is the line $AB$ itself.
questions.solution_md: False. The perpendicular bisector crosses $AB$ at right angles at its mid-point. A point of the line $AB$ other than the mid-point is nearer to one end than the other, so it is not equidistant.

questions.stem_md: A circle is the locus of the points that are at a given distance from a given point, the centre.
questions.solution_md: True. This is the definition: the given distance is the radius, and every point at that distance is on the circle.

questions.stem_md: A straight line and a circle can have exactly one point in common.
questions.solution_md: True. When the line is at a distance from the centre equal to the radius, it touches the circle at one point (a tangent). Otherwise they meet in two points or not at all.

questions.stem_md: The locus of points $3$ cm from a straight line is a pair of parallel lines that are ___ cm apart.
questions.solution_md: One parallel is $3$ cm from the line on each side, so the two are $3 + 3 = 6$ cm apart.

questions.stem_md: $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, with $AB = 8$ cm and $PA = 5$ cm. The distance from $P$ to the mid-point of $AB$ is ___ cm.
questions.solution_md: With $M$ the mid-point, $AM = 4$ and the right triangle $AMP$ gives $PM = \sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The two lines that form the locus of points equidistant from two crossing roads meet each other at an angle of ___ degrees.
questions.solution_md: The two bisectors are perpendicular: the half-angles of a straight line add up to $90^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A path has two straight parallel edges $9$ m apart. A line of lamps equidistant from the two edges is ___ m from each edge.
questions.solution_md: The middle line is half the gap from each: $\dfrac{9}{2} = 4.5$ m.

questions.stem_md: The locus of the points that are equally far from two fixed points is the ___ of the line segment that joins them.
questions.solution_md: Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them: it is the line through the mid-point at right angles to the segment, and it is the locus.

questions.stem_md: A bisector of an angle of $84^\circ$ makes an angle of ___ degrees with each arm.
questions.solution_md: The bisector halves the angle: $\dfrac{84}{2} = 42$, so each part is $42^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: All the points that are $4$ cm from a fixed point $O$ lie on a ___ of radius $4$ cm.
questions.solution_md: The locus of points at a fixed distance from a fixed point is a circle: here the circle with centre $O$ and radius $4$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The perpendicular bisector of a segment $AB$ passes through the ___ of $AB$.
questions.solution_md: By construction it cuts $AB$ at right angles at its mid-point, which is the one point of $AB$ equidistant from $A$ and $B$.

questions.stem_md: A buoy $P$ is the same distance from piers $A$ and $B$, which are $16$ m apart, and it is $17$ m from each pier. Find its distance from the line $AB$, in m.
questions.solution_md: $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, so the foot of its perpendicular to $AB$ is the mid-point $M$ with $AM = 8$ m: $\sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$.

questions.stem_md: A point lies on the bisector of a $40^\circ$ angle between two straight rails, $10$ cm from the vertex. Find its distance from each rail, to the nearest $0.1$ cm.
questions.solution_md: The bisector makes $20^\circ$ with each rail, so the distance is $10 \sin 20^\circ = 3.4$ cm.

questions.stem_md: On a number line of survey markers, the points $A(-3, 0)$ and $B(5, 0)$ are given. A marker $P(x, y)$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$. Find $x$.
questions.solution_md: The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is the vertical line through the mid-point, whose $x$-coordinate is $x = \dfrac{-3 + 5}{2} = 1$, so every such marker has $x = 1$.

questions.stem_md: A rectangular plot has corners $A(0, 0)$, $B(6, 0)$ and $C(0, 8)$ on a plan. A fountain is placed at the point equidistant from all three corners. How far, in plan units, is it from $A$?
questions.solution_md: The fountain is where the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $AC$ meet: $x = 3$ and $y = 4$. Its distance from $A$ is $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ units.

questions.stem_md: A garden plan is drawn to the scale $1 : 50$. A sprinkler waters a circle of radius $3$ m. What is the radius of that circle on the plan, in cm?
questions.solution_md: The real radius is $3$ m, which is $300$ cm, so on the plan it is $\dfrac{300}{50} = 6$ cm. In metres, $\dfrac{3}{50} = 0.06$ m, and $0.06 \times 100 = 6$ cm.

questions.stem_md: A paved cycle track has two straight parallel edges $5.4$ m apart. A line of reflectors is fixed equally far from both edges. How far is it from each edge, in m?
questions.solution_md: The reflectors lie on the line midway between the edges: $\dfrac{5.4}{2} = 2.7$ m from each.

questions.stem_md: A point on the bisector of the angle between two straight pipes is $12$ cm from the point where the pipes meet and $6$ cm from each pipe. Find the angle between the pipes, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: The perpendicular to a pipe, the segment to the vertex and the pipe form a right triangle in which $\sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{6}{12} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\dfrac{\theta}{2} = 30^\circ$ and the angle between the pipes is $2 \times 30 = 60$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: Surveyors set pegs $2.5$ m from a straight fence and $6.5$ m from a gatepost $C$ on the fence. Two such pegs stand on the same side of the fence. Find the distance between them, in m.
questions.solution_md: The pegs are where the circle of radius $6.5$ about $C$ meets the parallel at $2.5$ m. Each is $\sqrt{6.5^2 - 2.5^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6$ m along the fence from the foot of the perpendicular from $C$, on opposite sides, so they are $2 \times 6 = 12$ m apart.

questions.stem_md: Two taps $A$ and $B$ are fitted on a straight pipe $9.6$ m apart. A valve is to be fixed on the pipe at the point equally far from both taps. How far from $A$, in m, is the valve?
questions.solution_md: On the segment $AB$ the only point equidistant from $A$ and $B$ is its mid-point, so the valve is $\dfrac{9.6}{2} = 4.8$ m from $A$.

questions.stem_md: The second hand of a wall clock is $9$ cm long and turns about its pivot. Name the locus of the tip of the hand and state the diameter of the figure it traces.

answer.model_answer_md:
The tip is always $9$ cm from the pivot, so its locus is a circle with the pivot as centre and radius $9$ cm.

The diameter is $2 \times 9 = 18$ cm.

questions.solution_md: A fixed distance from a fixed point gives a circle; the diameter is twice the radius.

marking_scheme.step: circle, centre at the pivot, radius 9 cm

questions.stem_md: Describe how to draw the perpendicular bisector of a segment $PQ = 7.2$ cm using a pair of compasses and a ruler, and state which radius values may be used for the arcs.

answer.model_answer_md:
With compass point on $P$ and radius more than $3.6$ cm (say $4.5$ cm) draw an arc above and below $PQ$. With the same radius and the compass point on $Q$ draw arcs that cut the first two at $X$ and $Y$. Join $XY$: it cuts $PQ$ at its mid-point at a right angle.

The radius must be greater than half of $PQ$, that is greater than $\dfrac{7.2}{2} = 3.6$ cm, or the arcs do not cross.

questions.solution_md: Equal arcs from both ends meet only if the radius exceeds half the segment.

marking_scheme.step: equal arcs from P and Q cut at X and Y; XY joined

questions.stem_md: The two kerbs of a straight road are parallel and $7$ m apart. A line of reflectors is to be fixed equally far from both kerbs. Describe the locus of the reflectors and state how far it is from each kerb.

answer.model_answer_md:
The locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines is a third line parallel to both, midway between them.

It is $\dfrac{7}{2} = 3.5$ m from each kerb.

questions.solution_md: The midline of two parallels is parallel to them, at half their distance.

marking_scheme.step: a line parallel to both kerbs, midway between them

questions.stem_md: A trolley on a wide platform keeps exactly $2.5$ m from a straight rail $AB$ and may be on either side of it. Describe the locus of the trolley and state how far apart its two tracks are.

answer.model_answer_md:
The points at a fixed distance from a line lie on two lines parallel to it, one on each side, each $2.5$ m from $AB$.

The two tracks are $2.5 + 2.5 = 5$ m apart.

questions.solution_md: A fixed distance from a line gives a pair of parallels.

marking_scheme.step: two parallel lines, one on each side of AB, 2.5 m from it

questions.stem_md: Points $A$ and $B$ are $5$ cm apart. How many points are $3$ cm from $A$ and $4$ cm from $B$? How many would there be if $AB$ were $7$ cm?

answer.model_answer_md:
The points lie on the circle of radius $3$ about $A$ and the circle of radius $4$ about $B$. With $AB = 5$, the distance $5$ is between $4 - 3 = 1$ and $4 + 3 = 7$, so the circles cut in $2$ points.

With $AB = 7 = 3 + 4$ the circles touch, so there is exactly $1$ point.

questions.solution_md: Compare the distance between the centres with the sum and the difference of the radii.

marking_scheme.step: 2 points when AB = 5, with the circle argument

questions.stem_md: $A$ and $B$ are two sensors $8$ m apart. An alarm must be $5$ m from $A$ and the same distance from $B$. Find how many positions the alarm can take, and how far apart the positions are.

answer.model_answer_md:
Equal distances from $A$ and $B$ put the alarm on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, and $5$ m from $A$ puts it on a circle of radius $5$ about $A$. They meet in $2$ points, one on each side of $AB$.

Each point is above or below the mid-point $M$ of $AB$ with $AM = 4$, so its distance from $AB$ is $\sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3$ m.

The two positions are $3 + 3 = 6$ m apart.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicular bisector with a circle; Pythagoras gives the offset from AB.

questions.stem_md: Straight lines $AB$ and $CD$ cross at $O$ and make an angle of $80^\circ$. Describe the locus of the points equally far from the two lines, and find the angles that its lines make with $AB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The locus is the pair of lines that bisect the angles between $AB$ and $CD$.

One bisector halves the $80^\circ$ angle, so it makes $\dfrac{80}{2} = 40^\circ$ with $AB$.

The other bisector halves the adjacent angle $180^\circ - 80^\circ = 100^\circ$, so it makes $\dfrac{100}{2} = 50^\circ$ with $AB$. The two bisectors are at right angles: $40 + 50 = 90$.

questions.solution_md: Both bisectors; halve the angle and its supplement.

marking_scheme.step: locus is the pair of bisectors

questions.stem_md: Two parallel pipelines $l$ and $m$ are $6$ m apart, and $A$ is a point on $l$. A junction box must be equally far from both pipelines and $5$ m from $A$. How many positions are there, and how far apart are they?

answer.model_answer_md:
Equally far from $l$ and $m$ puts the box on the middle line, $3$ m from each. The circle of radius $5$ about $A$ meets that line in $2$ points.

Each point is $3$ m from $l$, so along the pipeline it is $\sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ m from the foot of the perpendicular from $A$, one on each side.

The two positions are $4 + 4 = 8$ m apart.

questions.solution_md: Midline and circle; right triangle for the offset along the pipeline.

questions.stem_md: Angle $BAC$ of a triangular plot measures $64^\circ$. A boundary post is placed on the line equally far from $AB$ and $AC$, $6$ m from $A$. Find its distance from $AB$ to the nearest $0.1$ m.

answer.model_answer_md:
The points equally far from $AB$ and $AC$ are on the bisector of angle $A$, which makes $\dfrac{64}{2} = 32^\circ$ with $AB$.

The perpendicular from the post to $AB$ and the segment of length $6$ m to $A$ form a right triangle with hypotenuse $6$.

The distance is $6 \sin 32^\circ = 3.2$ m.

questions.solution_md: Bisector; right triangle with the half-angle.

questions.stem_md: A sprinkler at $A$ throws water $3$ m. A straight hosepipe $l$ lies $1.8$ m from $A$. How many points on the hosepipe are watered at the full $3$ m reach, and how far apart are they?

answer.model_answer_md:
The points are on the circle of radius $3$ about $A$ and on the line $l$, which is $1.8 < 3$ from the centre, so they are $2$ points.

Half the distance between them is $\sqrt{3^2 - 1.8^2} = \sqrt{5.76} = 2.4$ m (the perpendicular from $A$ to $l$ meets it at the mid-point).

They are $2 \times 2.4 = 4.8$ m apart.

questions.solution_md: Circle and line; the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord.

marking_scheme.step: 2 points: the line is inside the circle

questions.stem_md: On a plan, two survey pegs are at $A(1, 2)$ and $B(7, 10)$. Find the equation of the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The locus is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. The mid-point is $\left(\dfrac{1 + 7}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 10}{2}\right) = (4, 6)$.

The gradient of $AB$ is $\dfrac{10 - 2}{7 - 1} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, so the gradient of the bisector is $-\dfrac{3}{4}$.

$y - 6 = -\dfrac{3}{4}(x - 4)$, that is $4y - 24 = -3x + 12$, so the equation is $3x + 4y = 36$.

questions.solution_md: Mid-point and negative reciprocal gradient; or equate PA squared and PB squared.

questions.stem_md: Construct triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 6$ cm, $\angle B = 60^\circ$ and $AB = 4.5$ cm. Draw the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$ and mark the point $P$ where it meets $BC$. Measure $BP$ and say what kind of triangle $ABP$ is.

answer.model_answer_md:
Draw $BC = 6$ cm, make $\angle CBX = 60^\circ$ and cut $BA = 4.5$ cm; join $AC$.

Draw the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ (arcs of equal radius from $A$ and $B$). It meets $BC$ at $P$.

Measuring gives $BP = 4.5$ cm. Since $PA = PB$ (locus) and $\angle B = 60^\circ$, triangle $ABP$ is equilateral, so $BP = AB = 4.5$ cm.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicular bisector of AB meets BC; an isosceles triangle with a 60 degree angle is equilateral.

questions.stem_md: Draw an angle $ABC = 76^\circ$. Draw the locus of points equidistant from $BA$ and $BC$, and the locus of points $4.5$ cm from $B$. Mark the point $P$ where the two loci meet inside the angle and measure its distance from $BA$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Draw $\angle ABC = 76^\circ$ with arms of $7$ cm.

Draw the bisector of $\angle ABC$ (making $38^\circ$ with each arm) and a circle (arc) of radius $4.5$ cm about $B$.

The arc cuts the bisector at $P$ inside the angle.

The perpendicular from $P$ to $BA$ measures $4.5 \sin 38^\circ = 2.8$ cm, which is also the distance from $P$ to $BC$.

questions.solution_md: Bisector and circle; distance from the half-angle sine.

questions.stem_md: Two flagpoles $A$ and $B$ stand $7$ m apart. A banner must hang the same distance from both poles and $4$ m from $A$. Using a scale drawing, find the possible positions of the banner and the distance between them, to $0.1$ m.

answer.model_answer_md:
Draw $AB = 7$ cm (scale $1$ cm to $1$ m) and the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Draw an arc of radius $4$ cm about $A$.

The arc cuts the bisector at two points, $P$ and $Q$, one on each side of $AB$.

Each point is $\sqrt{4^2 - 3.5^2} = \sqrt{3.75} \approx 1.94$ m from $AB$ (taking $AM = 3.5$).

The positions are $2 \times 1.94 \approx 3.9$ m apart.

questions.solution_md: Bisector and arc; Pythagoras with half of AB.

questions.stem_md: Surveyors need pegs $2$ m from a straight fence $l$ and $3.5$ m from a gatepost $C$ on the fence. Describe the loci, say how many peg positions there are altogether, and find the distance between the two pegs that lie on the same side of the fence.

answer.model_answer_md:
Locus 1: the pair of lines parallel to $l$, $2$ m on each side. Locus 2: the circle of radius $3.5$ m about $C$.

Since $2 < 3.5$, the circle cuts each parallel in $2$ points, giving $2 + 2 = 4$ positions.

On one side each peg is $\sqrt{3.5^2 - 2^2} = \sqrt{8.25} \approx 2.87$ m along the fence from the foot of the perpendicular from $C$, on opposite sides.

The two pegs on the same side are $2 \times 2.87 \approx 5.7$ m apart.

questions.solution_md: Parallels and circle; chord of the circle at a given height.

questions.stem_md: A rectangular orchard has corners $A(1, 1)$, $B(7, 1)$ and $C(7, 9)$ on a plan. Find the coordinates of the point equally far from $A$, $B$ and $C$, and its distance from each of them.

answer.model_answer_md:
Equal distance from $A$ and $B$: the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is the vertical line $x = \dfrac{1 + 7}{2} = 4$.

Equal distance from $B$ and $C$: the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ is the horizontal line $y = \dfrac{1 + 9}{2} = 5$.

They meet at $(4, 5)$.

The distance from $A$ is $\sqrt{(4 - 1)^2 + (5 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$, and from $B$ and $C$ it is also $5$.

questions.solution_md: Two perpendicular bisectors meet at the point equidistant from three corners.

questions.stem_md: Two straight tracks cross at $O$ at an angle of $56^\circ$. Describe where a drinking fountain can stand if it is equally far from both tracks and $5$ m from $O$. How many sites are there, and how far is the fountain from the tracks at each kind of site (to $0.1$ m)?

answer.model_answer_md:
Equally far from both tracks means on one of the two angle bisectors; $5$ m from $O$ means on a circle of radius $5$ about $O$. Each bisector cuts the circle in $2$ points, so there are $4$ sites.

On the bisector of the $56^\circ$ angle (making $28^\circ$ with the tracks) the distance is $5 \sin 28^\circ = 2.3$ m.

On the bisector of the adjacent $124^\circ$ angle (making $62^\circ$ with the tracks) it is $5 \sin 62^\circ = 4.4$ m.

questions.solution_md: Two bisectors and a circle; half-angles 28 and 62 degrees.

(a) Construct triangle $ABC$ with $BC = 7$ cm, $\angle ABC = 70^\circ$ and $AB = 6$ cm, and measure $AC$.

(b) Draw the locus of points inside the triangle that are equidistant from $BA$ and $BC$, and the locus of points that are equidistant from $B$ and $C$.

(c) Mark the point $P$ where the two loci meet. Measure $BP$ and the distance of $P$ from $AB$.

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** The points equidistant from $BA$ and $BC$ lie on the bisector of $\angle ABC$, which makes $\dfrac{70}{2} = 35^\circ$ with each arm. The points equidistant from $B$ and $C$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, which cuts $BC$ at its mid-point $M$ with $BM = 3.5$ cm.

**(c)** The loci meet at $P$ inside the triangle. In the right triangle $BMP$, $BP = \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 35^\circ} = 4.3$ cm. The distance of $P$ from $AB$ is $BP \sin 35^\circ = 2.5$ cm, and $PB = PC$.

questions.stem_md:
A rectangular lawn $ABCD$ is drawn with $AB = 8$ cm and $BC = 5$ cm. A sprinkler $P$ is to be placed inside the lawn so that it is equally far from $A$ and $B$ and $5$ cm from $C$.

(a) Draw the rectangle and the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$.

(b) Draw the locus of points $5$ cm from $C$, and mark the points where it meets the first locus.

(c) State which of these points is inside the lawn, and measure its distances from $AB$ and from $A$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw $AB = 8$ cm and $BC = 5$ cm at right angles, complete the rectangle. Draw the perpendicular bisector $m$ of $AB$: it is the line $4$ cm from $AD$ and from $BC$.

**(b)** Draw a circle (arc) of radius $5$ cm about $C$. It meets $m$ at two points, $P$ and $Q$: with $C$ at distance $4$ from $m$, they are $\sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3$ cm above and below the level of $C$, at heights $5 - 3 = 2$ cm and $5 + 3 = 8$ cm above $AB$.

**(c)** $Q$, $8$ cm above $AB$, is outside the lawn (it is $3$ cm above $DC$); $P$, at height $2$ cm, is inside. So $P$ is $2$ cm from $AB$, and $PA = \sqrt{4^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{20} \approx 4.5$ cm.

questions.stem_md:
On a map drawn to the scale $1$ cm to $1$ km, two radio masts $A$ and $B$ are $8$ cm apart. A lighthouse $L$ is $1$ cm to the east and $5$ cm to the north of $A$ ($B$ is due east of $A$). A relay tower must be equally far from $A$ and $B$ and $5$ km from the lighthouse.

(a) Draw $A$, $B$ and $L$ and the locus of points equally far from $A$ and $B$.

(b) Draw the locus of points $5$ km from $L$ and mark the possible tower sites $T_1$ and $T_2$.

(c) Measure the distance of each site from $A$, and say which site is nearer to the line $AB$ and by how many kilometres.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Plot $A$, $B$ with $AB = 8$ cm and $L$ at $1$ cm east and $5$ cm north of $A$. Draw the perpendicular bisector $m$ of $AB$, the vertical line $4$ cm from $A$.

**(b)** Draw a circle of radius $5$ cm about $L$. It cuts $m$ at $T_1$ and $T_2$: $m$ is $4 - 1 = 3$ cm from $L$, so the sites are $\sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$ cm above and below the level of $L$, at $5 - 4 = 1$ cm and $5 + 4 = 9$ cm north of $AB$.

**(c)** $AT_1 = \sqrt{4^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{17} \approx 4.1$ km and $AT_2 = \sqrt{4^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{97} \approx 9.8$ km. The site $T_1$ is nearer to the line $AB$: it is $1$ km from it, against $9$ km for $T_2$, a difference of $9 - 1 = 8$ km.

questions.solution_md: Perpendicular bisector with a circle; Pythagoras for the heights and the distances from A.

questions.stem_md:
Two roads $p$ and $q$ meet at $O$ at an angle of $60^\circ$. On a map ($1$ cm to $1$ km) a ferry landing $X$ is on road $q$, $6$ cm from $O$. A rest house must be equally far from the two roads and $4$ km from $X$.

(a) Draw the roads and the locus of points equally far from them.

(b) Draw the locus of points $4$ km from $X$ and mark the possible sites of the rest house.

(c) Measure $OP$ for each site $P$ and the distance of each site from road $p$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw $\angle POQ = 60^\circ$ with the lines extended through $O$, then draw both bisectors: $b$ at $30^\circ$ to $p$ and $c$ at $120^\circ$ to $p$ (at right angles to $b$).

**(b)** Mark $X$ on $q$ with $OX = 6$ cm and draw a circle of radius $4$ cm about $X$. The perpendicular from $X$ to $b$ is $6 \sin 30^\circ = 3$ cm $< 4$, so the circle cuts $b$ in two sites $P_1$ and $P_2$. The perpendicular from $X$ to $c$ is $6 \sin 60^\circ = 5.2$ cm $> 4$, so the circle misses $c$: there are $2$ sites.

**(c)** The foot of the perpendicular from $X$ on $b$ is $6 \cos 30^\circ = 5.2$ cm from $O$ and the sites are $\sqrt{4^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{7} \approx 2.6$ cm either side: $OP_1 = 2.6$ km and $OP_2 = 7.8$ km. Their distances from road $p$ are $OP \sin 30^\circ$: $1.3$ km and $3.9$ km.

questions.stem_md:
A triangular flower bed $ABC$ has $AB = 5$ m, $BC = 7$ m and $CA = 6$ m. A water pipe $S$ has to be the same distance from the three corners. Use a scale of $1$ cm to $1$ m.

(a) Construct triangle $ABC$.

(b) Draw the locus of points equidistant from $A$ and $B$ and the locus of points equidistant from $B$ and $C$, and mark $S$.

(c) Draw the circle with centre $S$ through $A$, $B$ and $C$. Measure its radius, and show that $S$ is also equidistant from $A$ and $C$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw $BC = 7$ cm. With centre $B$ and radius $5$ cm and with centre $C$ and radius $6$ cm draw arcs meeting at $A$, and join $AB$ and $AC$.

**(b)** Draw the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ and the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. They meet at $S$, which is equidistant from $A$ and $B$, and from $B$ and $C$, so $SA = SB = SC$.

**(c)** With centre $S$ and radius $SA$ draw a circle: it passes through $B$ and $C$ too. Measuring gives radius $= 3.6$ m (the formula $\dfrac{abc}{4K}$ with $K = \sqrt{9 \times 2 \times 3 \times 4} \approx 14.7$ gives $\dfrac{210}{58.8} \approx 3.6$). Since $SA = SC$, $S$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, which the construction confirms by passing through the same point.

questions.solution_md: Two perpendicular bisectors meet at the point equidistant from all three corners; Heron gives the radius as a check.

questions.stem_md:
Two straight parallel roads $l$ and $m$ are $6$ cm apart on a plan. $A$ is a point on $l$ and $B$ is a point on $m$, with $AB = 10$ cm. A bus stop $P$ must be equally far from the two roads and also equally far from $A$ and $B$.

(a) Draw the roads and the locus of points equally far from them.

(b) Draw $A$ and $B$ and the locus of points equally far from $A$ and $B$.

(c) Mark $P$. Show that $P$ is the mid-point of $AB$, and find its distances from $A$ and from each road.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Draw $l$ and $m$ $6$ cm apart and the line $n$ parallel to both and $\dfrac{6}{2} = 3$ cm from each.

**(b)** Mark $A$ on $l$, and mark $B$ on $m$ so that $AB = 10$ cm (it is $\sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8$ cm along the road from the foot of the perpendicular from $A$). Draw the perpendicular bisector $s$ of $AB$.

**(c)** $P$ is where $s$ meets $n$. The mid-point of $AB$ is on $s$, and it is also halfway between the roads (since $A$ and $B$ are on different roads), so it is on $n$. The two lines meet at only one point, so $P$ is the mid-point of $AB$. Then $PA = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5$ cm, and $P$ is $3$ cm from each road.

questions.solution_md: Midline and perpendicular bisector both pass through the mid-point of AB.
